hook: A drug company holds the patent on a new allergy test, so for the next twelve years no one else may sell it. It could charge \$500, but few people would buy; at \$20 everyone would, but it would barely cover costs. Where does a monopolist set its price, and who loses when it does?

prereq.q: A price maker's marginal revenue curve lies
prereq.why: To sell one more unit it cuts the price on every unit, so MR is less than the price.

options: the total surplus lost when output is not the efficient quantity
the consumer surplus after a sale
prereq.why: It is the value of trades that would have helped buyers and sellers but do not happen.
The value of the last unit to buyers (P) equals its cost (MC).

figure.caption: The monopolist produces QM where MR = MC and charges PM from demand. Profit is the rectangle between PM and ATC; consumer surplus is above PM; deadweight loss is the triangle between D and MC from QM to QE.

chain.cause: The monopolist faces the whole market demand curve
chain.effect: its MR curve lies below demand
its quantity (QM) is smaller than the quantity where demand meets MC

chain.cause: It reads its price from demand at QM
chain.effect: the price is above marginal cost

chain.cause: Units buyers value above their cost are not produced
chain.effect: there is a deadweight loss, the triangle between D and MC from QM to the efficient quantity

ideas: Find Q where MR = MC, then go up to demand for P. Profit (or loss) is $(P - \text{ATC}) \times Q$ at that Q.
A monopolist produces on the elastic part of demand (MR > 0). Total revenue is largest where MR = 0, the unit-elastic point.
Monopoly deadweight loss: the triangle between D and MC from QM to where D meets MC. Consumer surplus is under D and above PM, out to QM.

Natural monopoly: ATC falls over the whole range of demand. Socially optimal price P = MC (efficient, but a loss); fair-return price P = ATC (zero economic profit). A lump-sum tax raises ATC only: P and Q stay put.

misconception.wrong: A lump-sum tax on a monopolist raises its price, because the firm passes the tax on to buyers.
misconception.right: A lump-sum tax is a fixed cost: it raises ATC but not MC. MR = MC at the same quantity, the price on demand is the same, and the whole tax comes out of profit. A per-unit tax, which raises MC, is the one that raises the price.

summary: A monopolist produces where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve above that quantity. Its profit is (P minus ATC) times Q; it can last because barriers block entry. It produces less and charges more than a competitive industry would, on the elastic part of demand, leaving a deadweight loss between D and MC from its quantity to the efficient one. A natural monopoly, whose ATC falls over the whole range of demand, can be regulated at P = MC (efficient but a loss) or at the fair-return price P = ATC (zero economic profit). A lump-sum tax changes ATC and profit but not price or quantity.
